content: Common wood sorrel is a plant belonging to the genus Oxalis, which is widely distributed across most of Europe and parts of Asia. During the spring, it produces small white flowers adorned with pink streaks, although red or violet flowers are occasionally observed. The plant's binomial name, Oxalis acetosella, is derived from its distinctly sour taste. The leaves of the common wood sorrel consist of three heart-shaped leaflets, each folded along the middle. Its stalk is typically red or brown in color. At night or during rainfall, both the flowers and leaves contract as part of their natural behavior. Historically, calcium oxalate, also known as sal acetosella, was extracted from this plant through boiling. However, the plant is mildly toxic due to the presence of oxalic acid, which is known to interfere with food digestion. Another species of common wood sorrel is Oxalis montana, which is native to North America. This species is found in regions ranging from New England and Nova Scotia to Wisconsin and Manitoba. While similar to Oxalis acetosella, Oxalis montana is distinguished by its noticeably notched petals. The common wood sorrel is sometimes referred to as a shamrock because of its three-leaf clover-like appearance. It is often given as a gift on St. Patrick's Day in celebration of this resemblance.
